subject: history
title: Raj, Resistance and the Birth of Congress
welcome_lead: Examine the high Raj, the rise of Indian nationalism and the shock of Amritsar.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on the Raj 1858-1919: Viceregal government, the Indian National Congress 1885 and the Amritsar massacre 1919.
final_note: You can now connect imperial governance to the politicisation of Indian society.

concepts.def: Direct British Crown rule in India from 1858 to 1947, administered by a Viceroy and the Indian Civil Service.
Elite administrative cadre, overwhelmingly British until late nineteenth century, governing districts and provinces.
Political organisation founded in Bombay in December 1885, initially moderate and loyalist, later spearheading the independence movement.
Curzon's administrative division of Bengal, widely seen as divide-and-rule, sparking the Swadeshi movement; reversed in 1911.
Legislation extending wartime detention powers, provoking nationwide protest led by Gandhi.
Jallianwala Bagh shooting on 13 April 1919 when General Dyer's troops killed several hundred unarmed Indians, a turning point against the Raj.

walkthroughs.body_html: From 1858 the Viceroy, advised by an Executive Council, exercised executive authority, while the Secretary of State in London held ultimate responsibility. The ICS administered districts via collectors. Indian Councils Acts (1861, 1892, 1909 Morley-Minto) gradually introduced limited Indian representation. The 1909 reforms also created separate Muslim electorates, embedding communal politics.

Founded in 1885 under A. O. Hume, the INC initially sought modest reforms. The Partition of Bengal (1905) radicalised politics, triggering the Swadeshi boycott. The Surat Split (1907) divided Moderates and Extremists. The Lucknow Pact (1916) briefly aligned Congress with the Muslim League. World War I mobilised over a million Indian soldiers, raising expectations of reform.

walkthroughs.h2: Rowlatt, Amritsar and the Government of India Act
walkthroughs.body_html: The Rowlatt Act (March 1919) extended detention without trial. Gandhi called a hartal. On 13 April 1919, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar; official figures give 379 dead, Indian estimates over 1,000. The Hunter Committee censured Dyer. The Government of India Act 1919 introduced 'dyarchy' in provinces but satisfied few.
